video_title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
gist: Clay's head of AI (auto-captioned as 'Jess') explains how Clay grew ~10x since late 2024 by betting on the GTM engineer, rebuilding its Sculptor agent as a coding agent on the Clay CLI and Pi harness, and deliberately making Clay headless infrastructure usable from Claude Code (now ~50/50 usage). Key economics: whole-market ICP scoring for ~$1,500, post-training only worth it at $10-100M inference spend, a coming Automod router, and platform risk shown by OpenAI's near-cancelled ChatGPT apps launch.

themes.theme: Clay's business trajectory and GTM-engineer focus

insights.claim: Clay has grown roughly 10x in revenue since late 2024, when it was about 50 people and $15-20M in revenue with small contract sizes; headcount is now around 600.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: A private GTM-infrastructure company scaling ~10x in two years signals strong demand for AI-native sales tooling; relevant to valuations of adjacent sales-data incumbents.
insights.quote: the business has basically 10 X since we joined

insights.claim: At the time of the Avenue acquisition Clay had nailed a PLG motion but had not yet moved into mid-market or enterprise sales; the acquired team's enterprise experience (DoorDash, AngelList, Ramp) was part of the rationale.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: PLG-to-enterprise transition is a key driver of Clay's revenue expansion and contract sizes.

insights.claim: Clay deliberately narrowed from a horizontal low-code spreadsheet tool (seven years old, with five years of 'basically nothing working') to a single persona, the go-to-market engineer, and credits that focus for its success.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Single-persona focus plus category branding ('GTM engineer') is a repeatable playbook for building durable dev-tool-like franchises.

insights.claim: Clay positions go-to-market as a creative endeavor and claims none of its competitors believe or act on that, using brand to build a community of power users.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Brand/community moat in a crowded sales-tool market may sustain organic word-of-mouth acquisition.

insights.claim: The GTM engineer role combines agent/prompt engineering, data engineering (list building, enrichment, transformation) and traditional software engineering, and is still sold into revenue operations teams; many practitioners come from software engineering or ambitious RevOps.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: A new budgeted job function means a new buyer persona for data, enrichment and agent vendors.

insights.claim: Clay integrates with data providers numbering 'in the hundreds' and deliberately stays generic rather than building point solutions, accepting that flexibility creates more ways for users to make mistakes.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Clay acts as an aggregation layer over databases like ZoomInfo, potentially commoditizing individual data vendors.

insights.claim: A large share of Clay's customers are not agencies but a broad 'everyone else' category who find Clay through word of mouth and brand, many still new to GTM engineering.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Broad SMB/mid-market self-serve base supports PLG economics but implies need for simpler, more automated UX.

insights.claim: Clay launched a web-searching, structured-extraction agent product as early as November 2023; these 'Clegents' that fill table cells remain a huge part of the business and most people think of Clay as Clegents.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Per-cell agent enrichment at table scale is the core monetized AI workload and drives inference volume.

insights.claim: Sculptor, Clay's orchestrator agent launched about a year ago on a tool-in-a-loop architecture, could add columns but was poor at long-horizon goals like building an outbound campaign that books 10 qualified meetings.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: First-generation tool-loop agents underdelivered on outcome-level tasks; watch whether coding-agent rebuilds close the gap.

insights.claim: Clay's key learning was that coding agents are really good: models operate well using Bash and Python, so Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a proper coding agent that uses the public Clay CLI inside a cloud sandbox.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that coding-agent harnesses are becoming the general-purpose agent architecture beyond software engineering.
insights.quote: it turns out coding agents are really good

insights.claim: Clay's new agent harness is built on top of the open-source Pi harness and customized, rather than built from scratch.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Suggests little proprietary alpha in harness building; value accrues to data/primitives and distribution rather than the agent loop itself.

insights.claim: Clay rebuilt its platform around a core data context layer called 'audiences' that entity-resolves CRM and Gong data into a canonical spreadsheet of customers and contacts, because the original agent lacked the context sales reps have.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Owning the first-party context layer is how Clay defends against being a thin wrapper; competes with CRM-centric data platforms.

insights.claim: Clay runs single-tenant data per customer despite obvious cost downsides, arguing that customers' enrichment needs are more custom and less duplicative than expected.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Implies higher per-customer cost structure but simpler architecture; a margin lever if multi-tenancy is later introduced.

insights.claim: Clay's rebuilt orchestrator agent is being rolled out broadly across every surface of the product, framed as its first-party agent and expected to drive much higher usage.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Usage-based expansion (the host suggests higher NRR) could follow from a more expressive agent.

themes.theme: Open platform vs owning the agent surface

insights.claim: Clay explicitly does not want its own agent to be markedly better than using Clay from external harnesses like Claude Code, aiming to be agentic GTM infrastructure for all agents.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: A SaaS vendor giving up the first-touch interface to be headless infrastructure; a template for how incumbents may survive agentic disintermediation.
insights.quote: we explicitly don't want our agent to be markedly better than just using clay and cloud code

insights.claim: Usage of Clay via external harnesses (e.g. Claude Code) versus Clay's own harness is much closer to 50/50 than the company expected.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Shows how quickly external agent harnesses become a primary distribution channel for SaaS; relevant to Anthropic/OpenAI agent ecosystems.

insights.claim: Clay's MCP team shifted focus to building a CLI, and internal demand for the CLI came from Clay's own GTM team who would not leave Cursor; Clay's sales team uses Codex for deal prep.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: CLI is emerging as the preferred agent integration form factor over MCP for coding-agent-native users.

insights.claim: The host argues that exposing a SaaS product as a great API means losing the first-touch interface, a stance he attributes also to Mark Benioff at Salesforce.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Watch whether SaaS incumbents trade seat-based UI revenue for API/agent consumption models.

insights.claim: Clay's Workflows product, launched this summer among '12 launches in 12 weeks', was initially confusing to users but is growing quickly as a share of activity versus tables, and most workflows are built with the CLI or agent.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: A shift from spreadsheet to agent-built workflows could expand Clay into Zapier-like automation territory.

insights.claim: The host argues Zapier did not evolve with the times, while Clay argues stateful workflows co-located with enriched data beat simple A-to-B data movement.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Legacy integration/automation vendors face displacement from data-native agentic workflow tools.

themes.theme: Inference economics, routing and open models

insights.claim: Running an ICP-fit question across Clay's 40-million-company dataset at ~1,500 tokens per company would cost about $1,500 with a cheap classifier-style model, making whole-market scoring trivially affordable.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Collapsing classification cost enables total-addressable-market scoring, expanding enrichment volume and potentially pressuring per-record data pricing.
insights.quote: it comes out to I think around 1500 bucks

insights.claim: Post-training and open-weight models only became viable for Clay in the past couple of months; the goal is to keep capability constant while cutting cost and latency by dropping a model class.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Signals shifting inference spend from frontier labs toward open-weight models for high-volume vertical workloads.

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf open-weight models such as K3 are cheaper than Opus by a good margin, and post-trained smaller models could reach Opus-level on narrow tasks, giving two jumps of cost reduction.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Margin pressure on frontier-model API revenue for routine enterprise tasks.

insights.claim: Companies jump into post-training too early; savings only matter at roughly $10M-$100M of annual inference spend, and exceeding frontier (Fable-level) performance in a domain remains very hard.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Useful threshold for judging which AI application companies can credibly improve gross margins via custom models.

insights.claim: Frontier intelligence still matters for orchestration and creative end-to-end GTM plays where output varies 10x-100x between best and average, while evals for simple enrichment tasks have been saturated for about a year.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Frontier-model demand concentrates in high-level orchestration; commodity tasks migrate to cheap models.

insights.claim: Clay will launch a model router called Automod because users hate the model selector; the selector will stay for power users such as agency owners.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Vendor-controlled routing lets AI apps arbitrage model costs, reducing end-user loyalty to specific labs.
insights.quote: our users hate our model selector

insights.claim: Typical enrichment budgets are $1-$10 per qualified lead and $10-$100 per booked call, depending on customer expected value.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the willingness to pay that supports enrichment and agentic prospecting pricing.

insights.claim: Clay does not dual-source inference but will probably do so now; its spiky, table-scale workloads (e.g. 50,000-company runs) required throttling, failover and pause/resume, with fairness to avoid large enterprises crowding out small users.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Spiky batch inference makes rate limits and provider reliability a real operational risk for AI apps.

insights.claim: Clay hand-rolls most agent durability on BullMQ (JavaScript) rather than Temporal or LangGraph, and the head of AI is unsure it survives another 10x of scale.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Possible future demand for durable-execution vendors as AI apps scale.

insights.claim: Clay uses ClickHouse in product and internally, Snowflake for analytics, Postgres for most hand-rolled product data, Dagster for some internal datasets, and LangSmith for agent observability.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Vendor-usage datapoint for ClickHouse/Snowflake; host argues the 'modern data stack is cooked'.

insights.claim: Clay launched 25-30 new integrations where the bottleneck was contracting, not engineering, supporting the host's view that connector businesses like Airbyte and Fivetran face pressure because integrations can be vibe-coded.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for standalone ELT/connector vendors whose moat was integration maintenance.

insights.claim: Clay reallocated about 25% of engineering for a month mid-quarter to launch as a ChatGPT apps partner, and OpenAI postponed the launch indefinitely two days before, reversing three or four days later.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Illustrates platform risk and chaotic decision-making at AI labs for partners building on their distribution.
insights.quote: Probably 25% of the engineering team for a month

insights.claim: The guest views AI as a platform shift comparable to early iPad apps, but argues nobody has yet figured out the 'platform' part, even though the AI shift itself is clear.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Distribution marketplaces inside AI assistants remain unproven; be cautious valuing app-store-style AI platforms.

insights.claim: Frontier models are 'still kind of dumb' in agent traces, e.g. retrying CLI commands with the same inputs without correcting, and are poor at diagnosing what went wrong in a long trace, so automated self-improvement loops don't work and Clay still hand-writes skills.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Capability gap in trace self-diagnosis limits autonomous continual improvement; a watch item for next-gen models.
insights.quote: the models are still kind of dumb

insights.claim: Clay's evals moved from LLM-as-judge on tool calls to use-case-based trajectory and output-quality checks; the aspiration is measuring second-order outcomes like whether outreach targets actually respond.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Outcome-based evaluation (as Sierra does) is the path toward outcome-based pricing in GTM software.

insights.claim: The host suggests AI vertical companies package bug reports into public benchmarks (as Sierra did with tau-bench verticals) to get labs to optimize for their domain; Clay is considering what a sales-optimized model or benchmark would look like.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Vertical benchmarks are a lever for app companies to steer lab model improvement toward their workloads.

insights.claim: Clay's agent determined how many YC companies use Clay in about 60 seconds, a cross-referencing task that would previously have required scraping, Snowflake access and Salesforce lookups.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Shows agentic analytics displacing manual BI work; also hints at high Clay penetration among YC startups.

insights.claim: Hiring people with hands-on production-agent experience is the hardest capability to find, especially in New York, partly because ChatGPT is only about four years old.
insights.speaker: Jeff Barg (Clay, Head of AI)
insights.so_what: Talent scarcity for agent engineers supports compensation inflation and acqui-hire activity.
